utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, if I could remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. van Lynden, good afternoon to you, sir. My name is Mira Tapuskovic. I am one of Miroslav Radic's counsel. In order for me to further familiarise myself with the role of your testimony here, can you please confirm that you have already testified in this Tribunal in other cases.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, this occurred in the Galic case and the Milosevic case as well. Would that be a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. van Lynden, do you remember when, precisely, you testified in those cases?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Mr. Milosevic it was in the autumn of 2003, and with Mr. Galic, either in early 2003 or in 2002. I think in 2003 as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You testified in the Galic case in January 2002. Your testimony was extensive in both cases. Each time you took several days. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember my testimony in the Galic case being longer than in the Milosevic case because my testimony in the Galic case was handed, in written form, in to the proceedings in the Milosevic case, and therefore the Milosevic case was shorter.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You talked to the investigators of the ICTY twice -- or rather, the Defence are in possession of two of your statements indicating that the interviews unfolded over several days. Can you please tell us where the conversations or interviews took place.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I was interviewed was in Vienna in 2000 or the beginning -- the first half of 2001. Later interviews later took place here in The Hague. This is the longer statement which was taken by a Nepalese lawyer, Tejshree Thapa.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. When you testified in the Milosevic case, you said that you teach journalism at the American university in Bulgaria. When you testified in the Galic case, you did not mention this. Would I be right to conclude that you left the practice of active journalism, as it were, between January 2002 and September 2003?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I left active journalism at the beginning of September 2001 when my wife was posted as ambassador of the Netherlands to Bulgaria. I was not working at the American university until September 2002. So for a year I didn't work, either in journalism or in academia.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Going through your statement, except for the fact that at the beginning of your career you worked for a Dutch paper, which unfortunately I'm unable to pronounce the name of. I seem to have a slight problem pronouncing Dutch names. You also worked for Washington Post, BBC radio, the Observer, and, finally, Sky News. All of your employers with the exception of the Dutch one, the Dutch paper, or rather, those who commissioned your reports and articles were non-Dutch newspaper houses, as it were.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't only work during my time as a journalist for the newspaper of The Hague, the Haagsche Courant, I also worked for a time for Dutch television -- national television news and for one of the Dutch radio stations, the NCOV. This is prior to the war in Yugoslavia, during the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is something that you spoke about in the Milosevic case, too. You talked about Baghdad, you talk about Iraq. You said that you were on both sides of the conflict, as it were, Iraq and Iran. Would that seem to be the case?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1980 and in 1984 I went to both Iraq and Iran and covered the war there from both sides, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you agree with me that in order to provide fair and accurate, even-handed reports, if you like, your duty as a journalist would be to put every story into perspective, especially in a wartime situation, to provide information originating from both warring parties or all the warring parties. Would you tend to agree with that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly agree that a journalist should try to put stories into perspective. It is not on the whole possible for a journalists to cover two sides of a war simultaneously. That is simply an impossibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While testifying in the Galic case, you said that you were first sent to Slovenia and that you, to all practical intents, were an eye-witness to what we in Yugoslavia usually refer to as the seven-day war. Would that seem be the case?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was indeed sent to Slovenia and was an eye-witness to some of the events in Slovenia. I was clearly not everywhere in Slovenia but I was an eye-witness to certain events, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in Slovenia throughout the duration of that conflict?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You informed the international public about the case when the Slovene Territorial Defence killed 45 young [Realtime transcript read in error "youngian"] JNA soldiers who were holding their hands up in the air as a token of surrender. Do you remember this incident?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of informing the international public of the killing of 45 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for the benefit of the transcript, on page 4, line 15, it should read "45 young JNA soldiers." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that Sky News, your employer at the time, if I may use the term since you told us that you worked as a freelance journalist, set up an office in Zagreb or Croatia. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a full-time staff employee of Sky News from 1988 onwards. I was not a freelance journalist ever during my time at Sky News. As I was not a freelance journalist ever during my time at Sky News. As far as I'm aware Sky News moved a team to Zagreb. I imagined working out of a hotel. I was never part of that team, so I don't know if they actually set up an office the same way as we did do in Belgrade. But I'm aware that teams were sent into Zagreb to cover the war in 1991 from the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my apologies for possibly hurting your feelings in any way about your job. Based on the documents that I had occasion to consult, my impression was that you continued to work as a freelancer throughout; however, let us now pick up where we left off. When you said that Sky News worked out of Croatia in a way, were you ever in touch with your counterpart in Sky News on the Croatian side of the border, as it were, and did you discuss anything that was going on in Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember ever being directly in touch with those working out of Zagreb. We would have possibly passed messages through the foreign desk of Sky News in London, but I don't remember having direct telephone conversations with those working out of Zagreb, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm about to say something that is quite apparent if one considers your testimony. You arrived in Yugoslavia in July, 1991, following a brief break after what had occurred in Slovenia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in Slovenia in June 1991 when I imagined, apart from the Slovenes, most Yugoslavs still considered Slovenia to be part of Yugoslavia. From Slovenia I was then -- when after about two weeks in Slovenia, I was then sent to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Following your arrival in Belgrade in July, were you stationed in Belgrade throughout or did you, on occasion, leave Belgrade, leave the former Yugoslavia possibly, or did you remain within the borders, as it were, of the former Yugoslavia throughout this period?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did leave in August 1991. I believe my original statement actually includes that because I was sent to Beirut, the Lebanese capital, for the release of the hostages that had been held there, some of whom were my personal friends, and I had lived in Lebanon so I was told to cover that. I was aware of a second period which I was away which would have been from the end of October during the first week or ten days of November 1991. And the next time I left was just before Christmas in December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This means that when you covered a war area you did not only cover that area but all the other areas of war and crisis or, in other words, wherever Sky News would send you to. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only other -- as I said, the only other place they sent me to which was not -- the war there had finished and the other time I was sent home for a break of ten days to two weeks. I was -- at that time I -- my family was living in Brussels, Belgium.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me when you first heard about the JNA barracks in Croatian territory being blocked?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tactic was first used by the Slovenes and I witnessed that being used there. When I precisely heard the first time that the JNA barracks within Croatia were being blocked, I cannot remember a precise date. But I imagine that the Croats used the similar tactics to the Slovenes at a relatively early date.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you then please explain what were your activities from July 1991 when, as you say, you were stationed in Belgrade to the actual outbreak of the conflict in Vukovar? Where did you spend this period of time?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, as I said in my testimony to the Court yesterday, initially I was sent to the Banija region and then on to the Krajina and to the town of Knin. I then returned to Belgrade, and from Belgrade at a certain moment left for Beirut and returned towards the end of August or the beginning of September and then started going into Eastern Slavonia, also covering a variety of matters within Belgrade, for instance, the lack of petrol and oil and political situation. And later on in the autumn, apart from going to Eastern Slavonia, we also flew to Montenegro and drove up with the JNA units that attacked Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout your time in Belgrade you had an office, as you said yesterday, an office that had been set up inside the then-Serbian television, state television. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. In -- when Sky News began in February 1989, an agreement was signed between Yugoslav television and Sky News, whereby Yugoslav television had the rights to rebroadcast Sky News for however many hours they wished and for a certain time, I think it was the third channel of state television in Belgrade, would broadcast Sky News 12 hours a day. The other part of the agreement was that Sky News could make use of the facilities of Belgrade television. They helped us during the Romanian revolution in 1979 [sic] and again when I moved to Belgrade in July 1991. We continued to have an office within Belgrade television until December -- the end of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This office of yours was within the TV Belgrade building or in a different building used by the TV station?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was inside the TV Belgrade building. It was one room.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you described your movements around Vukovar and specifically the route you took to get to the Vukovar Hospital. About that day when you were moving about Vukovar, was that the only route you took on that day or did you also drive through the suburbs?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously I drove through some suburbs to get to the city centre. I'm not -- are you trying to ask me whether I went to Borovo Naselje as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I am asking you about the city centre, as it were. Did you take any of the side streets or just the one main road?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we would certainly also be in the side streets and I think, as I mentioned in my testimony to the Court yesterday, we drove into town until we found the soldiers of the platoon of the guards with whom we'd been before, and we were with them on foot. So we took various streets in the city centre. But before you start asking me precise questions, may I remind you that this was my first walk in the centre of Vukovar and I had not been to the city before.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. The reason I'm asking you about this is back in 2002 you stated to the investigators that you had seen mines laid all over the place, including the centre of town. Do you remember stating that, sir?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see small fields of land-mines of anti-personnel land-mines close to the heart of the city, yes. And this was also I think shown on the footage that was shown to the Court yesterday and of JNA soldiers disposing of these mines by shooting at them. And I was with those soldiers when they did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. Thank you for assisting us with this. That was part of the first bit of footage that we saw yesterday, Exhibit 136 I believe. When you were commenting, I mean during the filming and not after the video was shown to you yesterday, you said that the clearing of mines was a very complex and sensitive task. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think what I said was finding them is a sensitive business, that clearing them was done in a rather easier manner, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's fine, but you also said that these mines were being cleared by the engineers units of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a reference a later piece of footage when in the heart of the city one sees an explosion go off. I'm not sure whether they were exploding mines or other ordnance that they had found in that particular house that we weren't told. But we were told this was an engineering unit. The soldiers who you see -- you saw yesterday on the footage were, I don't think, special engineers. They were simply soldiers who were clearing the mines by shooting at them. So that's two separate units and two separate pieces of film.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed, but as far as I remember you did tell us yesterday that you had been warned not to walk around on your own, but rather to wait to be accompanied by one of the JNA members because of the danger involved on account of all the mines being laid all over the place.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. We'd already been warned on the 12th of November when we first encountered the platoon of the guards that one of their soldiers had been injured that day before our arrival, either by an anti-personnel or a booby-trap. I cannot remember which of the two it is. My experience in other war zones has taught me that one has to be extremely careful in such circumstances as to where one walks. So that one wants to go with people who are aware that a certain area has been cleared, and for obvious reasons that one doesn't want to step on a land-mine or walk into a booby-trap.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you agree with me. The footage that we were shown yesterday, video number 1, you could see a soldier prodding the ground with some sort of a pole, apparently in search of land-mines. Would that seem to have been the case?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is fairly typical within armies around the world that one uses something of that sort if one is looking for land-mines.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also testified yesterday that the land-mines had been laid by the defenders of Vukovar. You remember that, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's indeed what I told the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If indeed those mines had been laid by Vukovar's defenders, would you then agree with me if I put it to you that this had been done in order to prevent anyone from gaining entry into Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was inside Vukovar. I do not know if they had land -- had put land-mine outside Vukovar. This was inside as part of, I would imagine, their defensive efforts to stop the JNA from moving further into the town. And we were told also by JNA units that the Croats had used anti-tank mines as well, often tying these to a plank and then using them from houses if they -- those houses were approached by armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about anti-tank mines, but what about land-mines? You can't use planks to control those from inside a house or any other sort of building or facility, can you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anti-tank mines are also land-mines, but -- no, for the smaller anti-personnel mine, which I think is what you're trying to refer to, those cannot be controlled, and that's the field that I saw being cleared on the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the minefield that you videoed and that we saw as part of the footage between the houses, as it were, yesterday. Right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that any passer-by would have been in danger of coming to grief if chancing upon such a surface with leaves or dirt concealing a trip-wire mine or anything of the sort? Would that not seem to be the case?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were not trip-wire mines that I saw, but anyone not aware that mines had been sown in this area would indeed be in danger of being injured if walking into that piece of land.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree, sir, that Vukovar's defenders had laid these mines across the streets of their own city, thereby preventing anyone from gaining entry into town but also cutting off their own exit, as it were, from the town?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't. I did not see mines over a road at any stage, nor did I actually see who laid this one minefield that was cleared. We were told by the soldiers we were with that this had been done by the Croatian defenders, but I can't say that with certainty because I didn't see the people laying it. But I never saw any street or road in Vukovar that had mines across it. As far as I am aware, the Croat defenders tried to keep a road open to the rest of Croatia for as long as they possibly could. And as far as I'm aware, the principal and last route they had was towards the town of Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm merely trying to go back to what you stated yourself, namely that the mines had been laid all over the place, including the centre of town, while yesterday we heard you stating that the mines had been laid by Vukovar's defender. Do you stand by what you said in your statement and what you testified yesterday?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that they had been laid by Vukovar's defenders. Yes, we were told that there were numerous minefields, but not across the roads. This was separate between houses, in parks, but not across any street or road. I never saw that while I was in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday when you spoke about weapons and armed forces, you said that you knew that Croatia did not have a regular army.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did not have a regular army in July 1991, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, from July 1991 on, what forces fought in Croatia with the then-JNA or against the then-JNA?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware but, as I have already stated, I was not on that side of the conflict. They had police units, special police units. There were paramilitary forces, and they slowly began force -- forming an army based on Croats, I imagine, who -- officers who had been in the JNA and who now decided to fight for the Croat state, the fledgling Croat state, in much the same way as an army was formed in Bosnia in 1992, which is something that I did witness at first-hand, the slow forming of a Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. We will leave Bosnia aside for the time being and focus only on the events in Croatia. Do you know how these forces that you just listed to us obtained weapons?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they must have had weapons, as they were the police. So again, these would have been light weaponry. I am aware also now - I'm not sure I was aware at the time - that -- of the allegations that the Croatian government had smuggled in weapons prior to the conflict beginning. They would have had -- for instance, the police forces would have had some armoured cars. And I imagine that from certain places within Croatia from certain of the JNA barracks, they may have gotten some weaponry from that. After July 1991, I imagine again that Croatia tried, as much as it could, to bring in weaponry from outside. And I'm certainly aware that later on in the war in 1993 or 1994, for instance, Mi-24 helicopter gun-ships were bought by the Croatian I believe from Hungary and those were used in Operation Storm in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There is no need to go in depth when I refer to the 1991 events and the weapons that the Croatian forces had in 1991. Since you did hear about weapons smuggling, would it sound familiar to you if I told you about the Spegelj scandal and the smuggling of weapons from Hungary?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to object here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: We are talking about Vukovar and now the Defence is again entering weapons from Hungary. I want the Defence to clarify the relevance of those questions specifically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's introduction of weapons to Croatia from Hungary, I would think.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Me, too, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do I correctly understand the import of your question, Ms. Tapuskovic? There's been no mention of Croatia in the particular wording of the question. I -- it seemed to me you were, by implication, suggesting importation from Hungary into Croatia. Is that what you are suggesting?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. You are right. I simply based my question on the answer of the witness. It was a follow-up question. The witness told us that he heard later on about the smuggling of the weapons. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that sufficiently indicates the relevance, Ms. Tuma. Sorry to interrupt you, Mrs. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, that's quite all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As for the smuggling of weapons from other countries into Croatia, you heard about that later. Now, during the time, that time when the events were taking place, did you hear that Croatia obtained the largest portion of its weapons by emptying the JNA depots which had been blocked in the territory of Croatia, starting from that spring of 1991?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the barracks being blockaded from the spring of 1991. I imagine that they did get weaponry out of certain army depots. Others, I believe, were blown up. There was one instance, at least, in the early autumn of 1991 when there was a major explosion within one of the JNA barracks or JNA depots within Croatia where ammunition and weaponry were blown up, that I can remember, but I'm not aware, of course, of -- I was not there. How much weaponry they may or may not have got. The information we were given in Belgrade, and I remember even General Kadijevic even mentioning it in his -- when I spoke to him, and that was in September 1991, that the weaponry that the Croats had smuggling into Croatia, that we're here talking about, relatively light infantry weapons. I'm not aware of anyone telling me that heavy weaponry, artillery, or tanks were being smuggled into Croatia during 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not distinguish between the light and heavy weaponry, Mr. van Lynden. I simply asked you whether you knew in which way they obtained their weaponry. I can see that this information, which is needed in order to provide unbiased reporting, you didn't have. Back in 1991, Croatia did not conceal this fact; it publicly spoke about the channels for obtaining weapons. Do you know that there was such statements made in public?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember those statements being made, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, can you give us an explanation that would be acceptable. How come that the defenders of Vukovar who, according to you, had only Kalashnikovs and pistols were able to hold off the JNA army for three months, preventing them from entering the inner area of the city?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that they only had Kalashnikovs and pistols; I said I only saw them with Kalashnikovs and pistols when they surrendered on the 18th of November. I have said that they certainly had land-mines of a variety of sorts, and I imagine that they also had some anti-tank weaponry, whether it was RPG-7s or heavier calibre, anti-tank weapons, that I'm not aware of. Your fellow lawyer of the Defence said yesterday that they had anti-aircraft guns. I did not see them having anti-aircraft guns. I never saw any kind of heavy fire being returned on to the lines of the JNA, either on the northern or the southern front of Vukovar. The fires, I said yesterday, was only heading in one direction; there was no incoming fire. That left me with the impression that they did not have any kind of artillery. As to why it took the JNA three months to take Vukovar, I would suggest that you ask the JNA that rather than an outside observer. But as far as I could see this was --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, I didn't ask you that. I just wanted to see whether you could explain how come the weapons that I mentioned were sufficient to defend the city for three months. I didn't ask you whether they had any heavy weaponry or anti-tank guns. My colleague asked you yesterday about the tanks that were destroyed. We will turn to that a bit later -- or perhaps we can do it right away. When you were travelling to Vukovar via Erdut, did you see a sign for a place called Trpinje?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have done, I don't know. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There's a road between Trpinje and Vukovar called Trpinje road. Do you know that on the 16th of November on the Trpinje road, a decisive battle for the defence of Vukovar took place?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. At the time I was on the southern front rather than on the northern front. I did not in November at all cross the bridge at Erdut. I only came through Sid, Tovarnik, and Negoslavci. So I was not on the northern front to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We're now discussing Vukovar as a city, not a broader area. This Trpinje road is perhaps 5 kilometres from the downtown area. It is also known as the graveyard of tanks. Did you hear of this term, which was coined on the 16th of November, two days before you arrived in Vukovar yourself?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard the term "the graveyard of tanks." What we had been told, as I mentioned earlier, and this we were told by JNA was that one of the tactics used by the Croatian defenders in the city was to tie land-mines on to planks of wood and at the last moment shove these out of the basement windows of houses in front of tanks or other armoured vehicles as they came up that street. But I was never told about a graveyard of tanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear on that same day, the 16th of November, about Blago Zadro, to which Croatians refer to as their hero, who was killed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have done at the time, but I do remember the name today.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now turn to events which took place in Vukovar itself after your arrival. Yesterday you told us that upon entering Vukovar on the 18th you went to Negoslavci where you saw that they were preparing to hold negotiations between the JNA and the defenders. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not enter Vukovar. Negoslavci is before Vukovar. I don't precisely remember the course of events, but I imagine we were stopped and we were told that the negotiations were taking place. I certainly remember seeing Mr. Sljivancanin there again, and he must have spoken to my field producer and explained to him what was happening. We then also met the ICRC delegate --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. Would you please try to focus on my question. I didn't say that on that day you necessarily entered Vukovar; I said that you came to Negoslavci and were present when the efforts were made to organise negotiations between the JNA and the Vukovar defenders. You confirmed that that was correct. Yesterday you said - and that was correct as well - that you did not enter Vukovar on that day. Yesterday you also said that three negotiators appeared from somewhere representing themselves as somebody appearing on behalf of the defenders. Can you tell us whether these people came wearing civilian clothes or military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I remember, they were brought on foot, accompanied by a few JNA soldiers. And as I remember, they were wearing uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the uniforms for us to the best of your recollection after all this time has passed.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were wearing dark green shirts and trousers. I don't believe it being camouflage uniform, but I think that they had a sort of camouflage waist coat -- or at least one of them. I think that there -- the leader of the delegation was the tallest of the three, but I don't have a precise recollection. They walked past us, and as I think I said yesterday I was not actually allowed myself into the room where the negotiations took place, only the cameraman. We included pictures of that, so I must have looked at the pictures on the 18th when we were editing the story, but as my recollection is, it was something just like a green uniform and possibly a camouflage jacket.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you observe whether they had any weapons on them?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly do not remember them carrying Kalashnikovs. Whether they were carrying a pistol on their hips, it's possible, but I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were there together with some other media representatives, did the JNA or somebody else present there tell you who these persons were, these three Croats, or was it a rumour that circulated among you, the journalists, stating that these were defenders of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had already been told in Negoslavci that there would be face-to-face negotiations with representatives of the Croats from Vukovar. I don't remember being ever told precisely the names of these people or their ranks, but we had been told beforehand that we would be taken to face-to-face negotiations mediated by the ICRC between JNA officers and representatives of the Croat defenders of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us yesterday that after that, you were taken to a location where you had been told the defenders of Vukovar would surrender. Then you told us all of these individuals wore civilian clothes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those carrying arms wore only -- and who laid down their arms wore only civilian clothes. That is correct. I don't remember seeing anybody wearing uniform. And the rest of those coming out of the town were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then please tell us, how long did you travel from Negoslavci to this small, white house in a deserted -- on a deserted farm? How did you get from Negoslavci to that house?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got there by car, driving in a convoy, convoy led by vehicles from the JNA. I can't remember precisely how long the drive took, maybe 15 minutes, maybe a bit longer. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like for you to tell me something relating to your visit to the hospital. Yesterday you told us that that was on the 19th of November. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time that we went to the hospital was on the 19th of November. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that that was in late afternoon, after 2.30. Is that right? A. In the afternoon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You stated quite clearly that neither in the hospital nor around the hospital did you see any members of the JNA or Croatian forces wearing any kinds of uniforms. Please tell us, what do you mean by "any kind of uniforms"? What kind of uniform did Croatian forces wear that you were able to distinguish?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By any kind of uniform, I mean any kind of military uniform and of a green or camouflage uniform variety. We did see some Croatians wearing those when we found the dead the following day. I did not see any uniformed men around the hospital when we arrived at the hospital on the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you saw nobody wearing any kind of uniform in the hospital on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no, I did not on the 19th see anyone inside the hospital wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived with your crew at the hospital, did anybody stop you at the door or on the premises asking you what you were looking for there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I imagine that when we entered the hospital we indeed must have spoken to people. It was pretty clear what we wanted there because I had a cameraman with me, which is pretty much recognisable to anyone. We were a television news team. As I said yesterday, we asked to meet the director of the hospital but did not do so and finally met this -- I specifically was asking to speak to someone in English of the hospital staff. And we then met this one woman doctor who did speak English. I cannot remember if we were stopped at the hospital entrance or after entering, but I think for anyone who saw us it was clear what we were and what we were there for.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you try to speak to any of the patients?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and I imagine that my field producer would probably have done a few short interviews with some of the patients who were in a position to talk. But these were -- I don't remember them precisely and we certainly didn't include them in the final story, the final report, that I did on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you then tell us who told you when you entered the hospital that the floors had been evacuated and how many patients there were in the hospital. Yesterday in your evidence you said that you'd been told this. By whom?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the English-speaking doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did this doctor, lady doctor, show you various corridors in the hospital and basement rooms, or did you start touring the hospital on your own?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that we did both. We showed us a number of rooms. She showed us, in particular, a number of patients and related their various -- the problems with those patients, including one baby child that had been severely injured. But I also remember that we were able to walk around on our own.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, based on the film we saw yesterday that you and your crew produced, the only thing shown there were corridors with patients. Would you please tell us, were there more patients along these corridors or inside rooms that were used for holding patients?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that there were patients everywhere. It was jam-packed with wounded and with people whom we were told were relatives of the wounded. I don't remember going into any empty rooms.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This lady doctor who spoke English, did she not say how many people, wounded people, were in the hospital, and did she perhaps say if there were any relatives of the hospital staff inside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think she is the one who told me that there was several hundred wounded, possibly up to 500 wounded inside the hospital. I -- we didn't count them nor did we have time to count them. And as far as relatives is concerned, the only thing I remember her saying is that her own -- I think her own daughter was with her inside the hospital. But I don't remember her saying that all the hospital staff had their relatives with them. That I can't remember. But I remember her talking about her daughter because this woman originally came from Vukovar and now said that she, with her child, would have to leave Vukovar. And at that time she believed that this would be forever.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm nearing the end of my cross-examination. Therefore, I would like to go back to what was going on on the streets of Vukovar on the 15th [as interpreted]. Before you went to the hospital, in your statement to the investigators you said that you had watched civilians leaving and that these civilians were being guarded by JNA soldiers in order to prevent any ill treatment that these civilians might otherwise have suffered on the hands of Serb paramilitaries. Do you remember saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I imagine you're referring to the 19th rather than the 15th, because the transcript reads "the 15th." But yes, indeed. In the centre of town we entered a large group of people being led back out of the city centre to the outskirts of Vukovar. We were told by the JNA that they were being led back because they -- that would be a normal thing to do once a city had fallen. I imagine these people were also interrogated, and they -- these JNA soldiers also said that they were protecting them, indeed, from the Serb militia that were also in the centre of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this. Indeed the transcript on page 23, line 20, seems to suggest the 15th. It certainly should read "the 19th." Thank you for that, Mr. van Lynden. My last question to you, sir, this is also something that is apparently if one looks at the footage you took when the defenders of Mitnica were laying down their weapons - and this is something you confirmed in your statement - the entire process unfolded peacefully with no jeering and no shouting. No one was being taunted. Do you think it would be fair statement to say that both the civilians leaving Vukovar and Vukovar defenders laying down their arms were being treated with due respect?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did indeed say that in my report that there was no jeering and no ill treatment that we witnessed, and that they were indeed treated with respect as far as we could see, but that was as far as them getting on the buses. What happened after that, we were not able to see. But what we saw, it was an orderly, organised surrender, and those surrendering were not mistreated.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I note the time, Mr. Bulatovic. Would you like to continue now for some nearly ten minutes or would you prefer to break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think a break would be fine in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. van Lynden would like a break now as well. We will resume then at just before 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. van Lynden. My name is Momcilo Bulatovic. I am one of Mr. Sljivancanin's counsel. Mr. van Lynden, before you were sent by your TV station to report on the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, Croatia specifically, what sort of information were you given, if any at all, concerning the situation in the area, concerning inter-ethnic relations, the intensity of armed fighting, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A file of newspaper articles had been prepared for me, and for the rest I was briefed by the people I encountered in Belgrade when I arrived there. As to what had been happening in the country, I met a number of journalists and political analysts in Belgrade who briefed me as to what had been happening in the country that year and in the previous years. I had also been in Belgrade in December 1989 before and after the Romanian revolution, when I had been in touch with a number of these people, and they had in fact talked about the situation in Yugoslavia then. And on several, two or three, occasions I had met Jaksa Scekic who is now the Sky News bureau chief in London. And we had talked about the situation in Yugoslavia during those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How long have you known Mr. Scekic for, Jaksa Scekic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him for the first time in the summer of 1989 in London when he came to conclude an agreement between Belgrade television or Yugoslav television and Sky News.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The other people you mentioned you were in touch with who provided some of your information, political analysts, a number of journalists, and some other people, are these people whom you had known for some time or did someone, Mr. Scekic perhaps, put you in touch with these people?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was either through Mr. Scekic or through my field producer, Zoran Kusovac, that I met these people. These are people like Zoran Sedovic [phoen], who died last year, Milos Vasic, people of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information from such people about what my colleague, Mrs. Tapuskovic, has asked you about, about Croatia illegally arming itself?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, I was told that there had been allegations made, that the Croats had earlier, in 1991, and possibly before that but I cannot remember if they said that or not, brought in arms into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps have any information received from this circle of people or otherwise that Croatia had laid siege to a number of JNA barracks seizing weapons from the barracks?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think we were informed that that had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In the framework of this same issue, did anyone tell you anything about the fate of the Varazdin barracks?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the name. As I mentioned earlier to your colleague, I'm aware that during the autumn of 1991 there was a major explosion at one of the barracks, one of the depots, within Croatia, but I can't remember the name of that and I cannot remember the precise names of these various barracks, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember an attack by the Croats against members of the JNA, some of the consequences being fatal; more specifically, do you remember an attack on JNA members that occurred in Split?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I do remember an attack in Split. If you were to ask me for a precise date, I wouldn't be able to give it. But I do remember of an attack in Split, yes. But as I -- that was in the summer of 1991, as I recall -- as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a member of the JNA was strangled on this occasion, and this person happened to be an ethnic Macedonian?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Once again the objection -- we're presenting the relevance to the Vukovar case. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps you can assist us there, Mr. Bulatovic. What do you say is the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the fact is the JNA intervened in the territory of what was then the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Croatia had main a unilateral declaration of independence, and all these details show us the mood prevailing of members of the JNA. Witness spoke about this yesterday, after all; however, I will not be asking any further questions of this nature, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. You'll move on. Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, your stay in Vukovar, October 1991, you said you drove into Vukovar or into the JNA barracks there in an APC. Can you explain why?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was there to cover what was happening, and we were told, as I recall, that access by the JNA to the JNA barracks had only just been achieved and to show us that the barracks was again in their hands, I imagined they said: You can go with us but it is too dangerous to go in your own soft-skinned vehicles. We were driving Volkswagen Golfs, and therefore they said: You can come with us in an armoured personnel carrier. That's how we went in and that's how we came out. I believe the trip originated in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Once inside the barracks, were you free to move about? Were you free to leave the barracks?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was audible to us that shooting was going on around the barracks, and we were told that it was not safe for us to move outside. When we arrived in the barracks, we went straight from the armoured personnel carrier into a building, as I think I described to the Court yesterday, something of a command and control room with maps and with radios. We stayed in that room, quite a large room, as I recall, for a certain period of time and then we left again. Therefore, the only thing I saw was within the APC when we drove into the barracks and then when we left again. But we were told and we heard that there was shooting going on, and we would therefore not have been safe simply walking around.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when did you meet these members of the guards brigade whom you were with on the 12th and the 13th and then later on the 18th, the 19th, and the 20th? Had you known these people prior to the 12th? Since you had been in Vukovar in October, did you have a chance to meet them then?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I recall, the first time I met them was on the 12th of November. My field producer, Zoran Kusovac, had met at least Mr. Sljivancanin earlier because he introduced me to him on that day. But for me, I only met them on the 12th of November for the first time. We did not meet any of them, apart from Mr. Sljivancanin, on the 18th, but we met them again on the 19th and on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The 12th and the 13th, you spent the entire night in Vukovar. Were you together with members of this unit throughout this time?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were they carrying out combat operations throughout or were they just staying inside this makeshift barracks or whatever it was. You did say it was close to the centre of town, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that it was close to the centre of town. They were staying in a normal house that -- where they had -- which they had taken over. No, they were not constantly engaged in combat operations, but they took us to various different houses across various streets. They took us out at night, when a patrol was sent out. And -- so we were in different houses in different streets. The one real combat operation that I am aware of them being engaged in happened on the morning of the 13th of November. As I have mentioned to this Court, we were allowed to watch one member or a couple of members firing a 60-millimetre mortar, but the lieutenant did not allow us to go with them on the operation itself to take out a house that, as I recall, I was on a crossroads, because he felt we would get in the way, endanger his men, and that we would also be in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You explained that. Thank you. During your time with this unit on the 12th and the 13th of November, 1991, did anyone from the unit deny you any sort of information that you wanted to know about? Did they ban you from taking any footage, videoing anything, while you were with them at their positions?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that I can recall. The only thing was that the -- as I said earlier, the lieutenant wouldn't actually let us go on this one operation, but I don't recall them ever saying: You cannot film anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You explained the reasons, yes. Thank you. What I want to know about is those permits that you had to apply for. What was the substance of those permits? What exactly did they say, permits allowing you into a certain area, those one-day passes or whatever you want to call them. Would you return these the next day or what became of them?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good question. I don't remember -- I mean, they were pieces of paper collected by my field producer. I imagine they had our names on it, that these names were checked in Sid. I had also a permanent accreditation as a correspondent to Yugoslavia, so I would have had to show that permanent accreditation paper, but I don't remember whether these papers, that we had to hand them back in or what happened to them afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that for a while you went to Belgrade to obtain permission and later on you needed to go to Sid. When did this time come when you had to go to Sid as well to get another permit, if my understanding of what you testified is correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, from the first moment that we entered the southern -- the -- from the south of Vukovar, we always had to pass by this office in Sid. I don't remember any similar office being on the northern side. It may be that our original trip when we entered Tovarnik and Ilaca, as I think it's called, that at that time there was not yet the office in Sid. But certainly in November we had to pass by that office in Sid as well. So you had to go to both, first the Ministry of Defence in Belgrade the night before, and then Sid on the day itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Aside from you, the Sky News reporter, was it ever the case that you were in Sid at the same time as some other foreign journalists?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect that was the case, but I don't have any recollection of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The 12th and the 13th you reached Vukovar from Sid. Did you drive in your Golf car or did you get there using a different means of transport? And if so, secured by whom exactly?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We drove in our vehicles, two Volkswagen Golfs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were you accompanied by anyone?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not until we reached -- but I imagine that we drove to the JNA barracks. I don't recall precisely where we met Mr. Sljivancanin. My recollection is that from then on somebody was told to go with us to bring us to the platoon commander to whom we went and with whom we spent the next 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please go into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, let us now turn to the 18th of November, 1991. You already touched upon this, but it remained unclear to me. Where and when did you receive information stating that there would be some kind of a surrender, that something interesting would happen? Can you specify what time it was?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't specify a precise time, but -- as far as I can recall, we were told that in Negoslavci. We were stopped. We met Mr. Sljivancanin. As I've said before, we were introduced to the ICRC delegate, and we were told negotiations for surrender would take place. As far as I can recall that, we were told all this when we arrived in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In front of the little white house where the negotiations were held between the representatives of the so-called Croatian army and representatives of the JNA, were there any other foreign journalists?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I recall, Michael Nicholson from ITN, with a team and Martin Bell of the BBC with his team. If there were other foreign journalists there, I don't remember them, and there were a number of Serb journalists there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were all of the journalists banned from entering the negotiations or was it only you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, the agreement was that we could allow our cameramen to enter for a little while to film at the beginning of the negotiations and that they would then -- the cameramen would have to leave, the negotiations would take place, and that the journalists were told to stay outside. It was the -- I should add here also for the Judges that it was the habit in the former Yugoslavia, for instance, at meetings of the federal Presidency that only a camera could go in and no sound was to be recorded at such meetings. Whether that was the case during the negotiations at the farm-house, I don't know. But it would not have been unusual for journalists not to be allowed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps, do you remember, who was it who set these conditions that applied to you journalists on that day, the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I imagine it was those hosting the negotiations, the JNA, but I cannot recall precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information indicating that such a request was perhaps put forward by the Croatian negotiating trio?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no information of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You stood waiting outside. Can you tell me how long did the negotiations go on, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember how long they took.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: After that you went back to the road where the members of the so-called Croatian forces had to lay down their weapons and then the civilians came and so on. Do you remember how long this process took, the laying down of weapons, boarding buses, and so on?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I imagine quite some time, but I don't have a precise recollection as to how long it took, nor do I have a recollection of it being first the military, people with guns, and then civilians. As I remember it, it was a mishmash of people, some with guns, some without. But if the figures are indeed correct that 4.000 civilians came out, it would have taken some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lynden, I'm trying to determine until what time you remained there. We have a footage with your concluding comments showing that it was still daytime. Therefore I'm interesting in pin-pointing the exact period of time, if you remember. If not, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a precise recollection as to when we left, nor do I have a precise recollection as to if we left and the whole surrender had actually been accomplished. It may have been that due to the fact that we had to drive back to Belgrade, edit, and file a piece, because of our deadlines, that we left earlier. I remember being there for some time, at least an hour, probably more, but a precise time -- and we certainly did not leave at night-time. I do not recall leaving at night. The usual thing that they would want us back in Belgrade by 6.00 at the latest. Certain days we were later than that, and it may have been that -- but I don't recall leaving that spot where the surrender took place at night. So we must have left there when it was still daytime.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you this: Do you remember whether after the negotiations which took place between the representatives of the so-called Croatian army and the JNA representatives, the representative of the International Red Cross gave any statement to the media?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall him giving an on-camera statement, no. He may well have talked to us, saying that the negotiations had been successfully concluded and that a surrender would take place. But I don't remember him going in front of the camera. In my experience, both before and afterwards with the International Committee of the Red Cross, it's very unusual for them to be willing to give on-the-record statements and it's actually also unusual for them to give off-the-record statements. They are very careful with their dealings with the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to that one representative of the ICRC, were there any other representatives of any other international organisation present at negotiations on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember him having an interpreter with him. I do not recall any other organisations, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 18th of November, 1991, at the time of the surrender of the so-called Mitnica Battalion of the so-called Croatian army, do you know whether any representative of any international organisation was present, the UN or any other organisation? Anybody else in addition to the representative of the ICRC? Do you know that Mr. Cyrus Vance was at Mitnica on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Vance, and he was not there on the 18th. I'm aware of him being in Vukovar on the 19th of November, not on the 18th. Nor am I aware of any member of his --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. van Lynden. I was only interested in the 18th. We will get to the 19th --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I finish with who was or who may -- I am aware that no member of Mr. Vance's staff was there on the 18th because I would have recognised them as well. It is possible that there was another organisation, but not that I can recall. I can only remember the ICRC being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, let us now turn to the 19th. We have the time-line described by you when you left Belgrade, how you travelled to Vukovar, when you arrived, and so on. When you met with the representatives or, rather, members of the guards brigade that you had been with on the 12th and 13th, do you remember what time it was when you met up with them?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the relatively early morning. I recall that some of them were still asleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You went to the water-tower. Was it at your request or did these people offer that to you, to go to the water-tower and record whatever you were interested in?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the water-tower with the captain and the lieutenant whom I've mentioned earlier, and they went into the water-tower and up the water-tower with us. Whether we went there because of our requests or because they decide to take us there, that I cannot recall. But it makes sense for me to -- for us to have wanted to go there because it was a high position which would give us an overview of Vukovar and the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please also tell me, do you remember whether you travelled in a military vehicle or was it your vehicle, in view of the fact that the lieutenant and the captain travelled with you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, they travelled in their vehicle and we travelled in ours. We simply followed them, but I'm not a hundred per cent certain on that. As far as I can recall, that's the way it went. Part of the time on that day we went in our cars; part of the time we went on foot. And I cannot precisely recall how I got to the water-tower, whether it was on foot or by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally go up the water-tower and were captain and lieutenant with you or perhaps a cameraman or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did personally go up the water-tower. The cameraman definitely went up there, because otherwise we would not have had the pictures. And as I recall the lieutenant came up. Whether the captain did as well, that I cannot remember. But I know the lieutenant did because we actually took -- the cameraman took pictures of the lieutenant looking over Vukovar from the top of the water-tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, did the lieutenant, whose name we're not going to mention, give you any statement when you were inside the water-tower for your TV station about combat, what took place, where, and so on?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me whether we did an interview with the lieutenant in the water-tower?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't mean an interview. I mean: Did he give you a statement? Did you record him giving you a statement and detailing something about the combat? Did that take place in the water-tower?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly don't recall having used that. The only thing I recall, the only interview that I recall having used with that unit is an interview with a man who I think was a sergeant in that unit, and that was an interview that we had taken on the 13th of November. We may have asked him questions in front of the camera, but I don't recall it actually being used in any report that we filed to London.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask about the 13th. I was interested in the 19th in the water-tower. Do you remember how long you stayed in the water-tower, half an hour, an hour?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would -- I suspect less than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And following that, where did you go -- or rather, who decided where you would go next? Was it you or the captain and lieutenant who were with you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a precise recollection of itinerary on that day that we went from A to B to C and what A, B, and C, D were. I remember going first, finding this unit. I remember soldiers showing us where the minefield was that we've seen and already talked about today. I remember them accompanying us into the centre of town when there was this large, further surrender of civilians that we have talked about. I recall that they -- we heard the music and saw the celebrations that we also saw in the film that was shown to the Court yesterday of people who said they were from Seselj's militia. But I don't recall the precise order of events of the 19th in chronological order, nor whether it was us who took the initiative or them. The one thing I do remember it was the soldiers taking the initiative, it was two things: Firstly, to show us the minefield and that that was being disposed of; and that they took us to these tunnels that had been dug under Vukovar and that they showed us those. That came because they told us about them and took us there. Whether with the other matters it was our initiative, that I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Now the hospital and the trip to the hospital, was it your initiative or was it that the troops went there and you decided to go with them, to accompany them, or did somebody else tell you to go there? How did you go to the hospital on the 19th, at whose initiative?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was something that we had asked to go to because we wanted to see what the state of the hospital was and the conditions within, what they were. Again, I'm not sure whether we actually went there on our own or whether we were accompanied by either the lieutenant or one of his soldiers. But that was something that we wanted to do. We were aware that there was a hospital in Vukovar and we wanted to reach it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'll accept that this was your request and that the army made it possible for you to go there. Did any of the members of the unit hinder your trip to the hospital? Did they try to talk you out of it? Or did they let you go there without any opposition, let you go and record whatever you wanted?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember them opposing our visit to the hospital nor them even trying to talk us out of going there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Once you arrived in the hospital on the 19th, if I remember well, you said that based on your recollection it was around 1400 hours. Do you remember - I think it was 1400 hours or 1430, that's what you said yesterday - do you remember, once you got to the hospital did any of the medical personnel of the hospital leave the hospital prior to you entering it and talk to you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I think I've mentioned, I don't have a precise recollection of the time we arrived at the hospital and I have no recollection of someone coming out of the hospital and talking to us outside the hospital. I -- my recollection is of talking to people inside the hospital, in the basement of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the medical staff members giving you the number of patients in the hospital and the make-up of patients prior to you entering the hospital? Let me assist you.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the army showed minefields to you and that they used an unusual way to clear the mines. Did the army also tell you about all of the locations of minefields? Did they tell you that, you being a war journalist? Did they tell you about all the locations, directions, and so on?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They took us to this one field that I remember and that we filmed. It was, for me, the first time that I had ever seen soldiers clearing a minefield in that manner, and therefore it was unusual for me. They warned us that there would be other mines strewn around and that we had to be careful where we walked and where we drove. And as far as possible, if we were to drive anywhere, that we should take the tracks of vehicles that had got just before us; that's normal in a war zone. And that you are careful where you walk. And as much as possible, also because I was responsible for the lives of three other people, it made sense for us, therefore, to go around accompanied by people who knew the town better than we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in the hospital in Vukovar, you talked to the lady doctor, patients of the hospital. Did you know at that time or prior to that time that there were any wounded members of the JNA in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, you said yesterday that you remained in the hospital for about an hour. Once you left, did somebody give you any statement there, upon leaving hospital? Did any of the medical staff give you any kind of a statement pertaining to the number of patients and so on?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The doctor, who spoke English and that we spoke to, we interviewed on camera on a number of different matters. I'm not sure whether on camera she would have told us how many patients she believed to be in the hospital, but it is certainly a figure we would have asked her about. Quite apart from that, the field producer would have also asked that question to other people who only spoke Serbo-Croat, a language that I do not speak. So we would have had that information. But that was not on leaving, but that was while we were there. I don't remember anyone on leaving, when we were leaving, wishing to make a separate statement to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that on the 19th you saw in front of the hospital my client and Mr. Borsinger, a representative of the ICRC. Could you specify the time of the day. How long prior to your departure for Belgrade, half an hour, 45 minutes, one hour?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot specify a precise time of day. It would certainly have been in the afternoon. I remember that we were in something of a hurry. I had to do a piece to camera, otherwise known as a stand-up or when the correspondent speaks directly to the camera because I hadn't done one prior to that time, and we had to leave back to Belgrade to edit and file the piece. So it would have been for us sometime in the afternoon, in the later afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Once you left the hospital on the 19th, before you recorded on camera your final comments, could you please describe to us the atmosphere in front of the hospital, around the hospital. Were there any civilians there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any clear recollection of what you called an atmosphere outside. There must have been some other people there. There were those that -- that we -- I recall seeing there, your client and the ICRC delegate. There must have been probably some more soldiers, but I don't -- I mean no major crowd or anything of that nature. I remember that the other two crews from BBC and ITN were also there. I remember being concentrated on doing a piece to camera as quickly as possible and then for us to leave Vukovar and drive back to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When I asked you, Mr. van Lynden, just a little bit ago about Mr. Vance you said yourself that you knew that he was in Vukovar on the 19th of November, 1991. Since he was an important international figure visiting Vukovar, did you report on his visit to Vukovar and on the talks that he had while in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, and for the following reasons. Mr. Vance, when he arrived for the first time in the former Yugoslavia initially refused to speak to journalists apart from at the airport on his arrival and his departure. At a certain moment on a Sunday we were invited to have an interview with Mr. Vance, on-camera interview. And a sort of deal was made after that that Mr. Vance would see me on a very regular basis, often for off-the-record conversations in which he would tell me what he had been up to and I would tell him what I had been up to and what I had seen. I was aware that he was going to be there on the 19th of November, but I felt that at that moment the story was the first time that journalists were able to see Vukovar and the centre of Vukovar and what had happened there and that -- I was aware also that Martin Bell, my -- of the BBC, did go to cover the Cyrus Vance visit. There were very few of us in the town, so therefore it made sense for me to concentrate on other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember that on the 19th of November, 1991, after you had left the hospital one of the members of the International Red Cross gave a statement to you or any of the other journalists who were present following the conversation with Mr. Sljivancanin that you have just described?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which conversation? I haven't described a conversation.
