utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th you said on your way out of the hospital you saw Mr. Sljivancanin talk to a representative of the ICRC. My question to you is: Did any of those people you saw on the 19th give you or any of the other reporters present there a statement?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not to me, and I do not recall whether a statement was given -- I don't remember seeing any statement being given to other journalists. It may have done after we left, but obviously I would not have seen that. But no statement was given to me, either by Mr. Sljivancanin or by the ICRC representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, your report you standing outside the hospital, directly speaking to camera, was that the last report or the last footage you took in Vukovar on the 19th of November, 1991, do you remember that, the one with you standing outside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, yes, that's the last thing we shot and then we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we now please play a part of the video that has been disclosed to us pursuant to Rule 66 by the OTP? I believe it was tendered into evidence yesterday. I'm talking about V0006475-1-A. I would then like to ask Mr. van Lynden to have a look, and then after that I have a single question in relation to this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's either Exhibit 136 or 138. 138 is the very short extract. Is it that or the longer video?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 136, the longer one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: "Aernaut van LYNDEN: That still exists between the Serbs and Croats that lay dormant during 45 years of peace that has now expressed its in a mutual commitment to a war, commitment which does not appear to have been satisfied even after three months of fighting here. Aernaut van Lynden, Sky News."

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, you have just seen this, I trust. Did you leave for Belgrade immediately after this final comment and is this indeed the last piece of footage that you recorded in Vukovar during the 19th? Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that's the way it happened, that we filmed inside the hospital first. And when we came out of the hospital I did the piece to camera and that we then left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So the contact between Veselin Sljivancanin and the ICRC man takes place before you make this final comment to camera, when you saw them talking outside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There I did -- it may be that we saw them after I'd finished this, but we were simply leaving. There I don't have a precise time-frame in my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But you left right after this, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, yes, this is the last thing that I filmed on the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let us move on to the 20th now, the 20th of November, 1991, your arrival at the hospital. You said that somewhere along the way you had met this lieutenant from a guards brigade, if my understanding and recollection of what you said yesterday is correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've already discussed him and his name here in the court today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I am not allowed to use his name in a public session, on account of protective measures. I won't go into that now. I will from now be referring to him as "lieutenant" and you know who I mean. Therefore, this lieutenant, did you reach the hospital with him on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I can't precisely recall if we went with him or without him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This was the morning of the 20th. You reached the hospital at about 9.00 or 10.00, I believe?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the morning of the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you arrived did you notice Veselin Sljivancanin there or was it a little later? This remains somewhat unclear because in your testimony you said: "Later on we saw Sljivancanin." I want to know about the time-line between your arrival and the point in time when you spotted him.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question, but I'm not really able to answer it. I cannot remember the precise chronological order that things developed on that day. He may have been there when we arrived. He may have arrived after we had arrived; that I don't remember precisely. As far as I can recall, he came after we had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see when the ICRC man arrived?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's the same situation. I -- I do not have a precise chronological memory of whether people arrived after us or were already there when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The discussion that takes place on this day between Mr. Sljivancanin and the ICRC man, where exactly does this take place, near the hospital's main entrance, in the vicinity of the hospital, out in the street somewhere near one of the hospital's entrances, and how far from where you were standing?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just about -- just in front of one of the entrances of the hospital is my recollection. How far away we were standing? Well, close enough for my cameraman to be able to film close-ups of both gentlemen, so not that far away. But not in a position that I could precisely hear what was being said between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you specify how long this discussion took, them talking in the street?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that they had spoken in the street; I said that they had spoken just outside one of the entrances to the hospital. And I do not have a precise recollection as to how long this conversation took place, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you perhaps remember something about this discussion? After how long did the ICRC man take the unusual decision to make that statement to you that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me and to the other cameras that was -- that were there; it was not to me individually or to Sky News but also to the BBC and to the ITN cameraman and to the other journalists there. I'm not sure whether he spoke to us first or whether Mr. Sljivancanin spoke to us first. Both gentlemen spoke to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was Martin Bell, the BBC reporter, there too on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. And he's also in the pictures that the Tribunal was shown yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You spent some time outside the hospital on the 20th watching the evacuation take place. Do you remember how long you remained there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have a precise recollection of the time. It must have been several hours at least, but I don't have a precise recollection. As far as my recollections go, the buses only left towards the end of the afternoon. So we must have spent a good few hours there. I do remember wandering around the hospital grounds, and during that period we found all those dead bodies that had not been buried. We must have been there five, six, seven hours, something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Aside from this conversation that Mr. Sljivancanin had with the ICRC man outside the hospital, did you see any other conversation between Mr. Sljivancanin and the ICRC man in a different place perhaps?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I can immediately recall, no. Not on that day. On other days, yes. But on the 20th, if you're referring to the 20th, that's the only conversation that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th, did you perhaps hear from anyone around the hospital or from one of the JNA members that on the 19th, on the evening of the 19th, four JNA soldiers had come to grieve because they stepped on mines in the vicinity of the hospital, just around the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not told that. And I'm surprised that you name it because it's the kind of thing that the lieutenant, who we won't name, would have told us, as he did immediately when we encountered him on the 12th of November, that one of his men had been wounded. He did not inform us that -- as far as I can recall today that four JNA soldiers had been wounded there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, can you please explain about the evacuation which you filmed and watched. It lasted way into the afternoon. It had commenced in the morning, I understand. Were the JNA members helping along with the evacuation by helping to carry the wounded and stretchering them into ambulances or doing anything along these lines?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember precisely a time when the evacuation began, let me first put that straight; and yes, I do remember seeing JNA soldiers helping in the evacuation of the wounded. And as far as I can recall, most of the ambulances were military ambulances, not civilian ambulances.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps notice health workers, the medical staff of the Vukovar Hospital, during the evacuation? If so, what were they doing? Were they just standing idly by, were they helping along, or what exactly? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a precise recollection of who was doing what on that day. I mean, the evacuation was done. Those who needed to be stretchered out of the hospital were stretchered out. Precisely who were doing the carrying, I don't know. I do recall that some soldiers helped. I imagine that some of the staff from the hospital helped. Then there was the mass evacuation of what I would call the walking wounded, and civilians who were not wounded in any direct way who walked to the buses. But I don't have a precise recollection as to whom at any moment was doing what.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. You were in Vukovar from the early morning on the 20th to the late afternoon hours. Did you know that in Vukovar on the 20th, 1991, there were persons called Goran Hadzic and Zeljko Raznjatovic, better known as Arkan?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met both Goran Hadzic and Mr. Raznjatovic, as I've already testified to this Court. I do not remember being told that they were in Vukovar on the 20th of November and I certainly did not see them myself in Vukovar on the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: About the 20th or perhaps the 21st, do you happen to know that on the 20th in Vukovar a session of the SAO Krajina government was held? Is this something that you knew about?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say you had occasion to meet both Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and Goran Hadzic. Under what circumstances, respectively?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I met them was in Belgrade during a night I was woken at about 1.00 or half past 1.00 in my hotel room. At that time we were staying at the Intercontinental Hotel. And a man who had met with my field producer earlier that week and who spoke English asked me to come down because he said there was an important meeting for him to take me to. As a correspondent in Beirut where life was very uncertain and such meetings also took place, you take a risk on each occasion. But I decided to take the risk. I went downstairs. I have to add, the field producer lived in an apartment in Belgrade, and therefore was not in the hotel. I was on my own. The man I met in the lobby was wearing a western camouflage uniform and carrying a Heckler and Koch sub-machine-gun. He took me to a car, BMW, with German plates, as I recall Frankfurt. The driver of the car was also wearing a camouflaged uniform. I was then driven into the heart of Belgrade. When we stopped, there were a number of men, again in camouflage uniform, a group of 30 or 40 men, with their faces blackened also, carrying a variety of weaponry, and I was then brought into a small patisserie, which I was told later belonged to Mr. Raznjatovic. There were people there, having a coffee, or a slivovitz, a rakija, whichever. They were told to leave. I was given a cup of coffee, and then Mr. Raznjatovic, together with Goran Hadzic, entered the room and we had a meeting lasting, I don't know, I can't remember precisely, 30 or 40 minutes. Mr. Raznjatovic was the one speaking. He spoke relatively good English. As far as I recall, Mr. Hadzic speak English at all. So the conversation was very much between Mr. Raznjatovic and myself, and that was the first meeting I had with these two gentlemen. I had a further meeting with both of them in Erdut later on and had several meetings later with Mr. Raznjatovic also in Belgrade and once in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Several meetings. Could you perhaps try to be more specific. Was that in this pastry shop or a different location?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meetings in the Erdut area were at his barracks. The -- in Belgrade -- I think he came, actually, to the hotel. But here I don't have a precise recollection. But these are very short meetings, not anything of any length.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You've been around. You have toured many front lines. You have met many warriors. We are talking now about Goran Hadzic and Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. I would like to know what you believed their relationship to be like, their mutual relationship. Did they trust each other? Was there perhaps a certain amount of dissidence between them? Just your impression, based on your impression of their behaviour in your presence?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is purely an impression, but it seemed that the two were at least politically of one view. It seemed to me that the two men were quite different. One was a man who did not hide the fact that he led a militia and that he was comfortable with guns and with killing, and the other man, at least in my impression, was more of a political figure that us say, not a military figure. How close or not they were was very difficult for me to say in one meeting, where most of the conversation was only with one of them because I couldn't have a conversation with the other, as we didn't have a common language.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to one of my earlier questions you said that even after your return from Vukovar you were still in touch with some members of that unit with whom you stayed, the first time on the 12th and 13th and the next time on the 18th, 19th, and 20th of November. What I want to know is: While talking to those people, did they ever tell you that they had been fired at from the direction of the Vukovar Hospital ever during their time there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to set the record straight, we didn't encounter them on the 18th of November. But your basic question, the answer is: No, I do not recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to your basic question as to whether they had ever said to us that they had been shot at from the hospital, the answer to that is: I do not recall them ever saying that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about the conversations and contacts that you had following your return from Vukovar. Did any of them perhaps object to any of the reports that you produced on behalf of Sky News surrounding events in Vukovar; and if so, what were these objections about precisely?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is again with the guards unit that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's the one I'm referring to. The captain, lieutenant, and the other officer. The people that you were in touch with.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing that has to be said is: They would not have been in a position to see my reports as they were broadcast because they were in Vukovar at the time and would not have had access to a television there to watch Sky News. I don't have a precise recollection, but I think on the evening that we went out to dinner with them that we actually showed them the reports that we had done on VHS. Major criticism, I don't remember any major criticism. If there was any criticism, it would have come from the captain, Captain Maric. There may have been something that he was not particularly happy about. I do remember that they laughed, as we did, that the only comment from the federal Ministry of Defence in criticism was the fact that we had filmed and included pictures of empty ammunition cases in the streets of Vukovar and they had told us that they didn't want to show the military leaving debris on the streets of Vukovar and the captain and the others thought that that was as ridiculous as we did. But I don't remember any specific criticism that any of them made of the reports that I did, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But there was fewer [Realtime transcript read in error "viewer"] criticism, as far as you can remember. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Viewer criticism? Am I getting the translation right here?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Fewer criticisms or minor criticisms.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a difference for the translators, please. There may have been. I can't -- I mean, I can't recall what was said in a -- one conversation more than 14 years ago as far as a minor criticism. I don't remember them being particularly angry. I think that they were perfectly happy of the picture that we gave of the unit and what they were doing on the 12th and 13th. And -- nor do I recall them being particularly unhappy with any of the stories that we had filmed on the 18th, 19th, or 20th either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is this time for a break? I will not have many questions more, but I don't think that I will conclude in the next five minutes or so. So perhaps this would be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will give you time to collect your final thoughts if we have a break anyway, Mr. Bulatovic. We will resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, in your evidence yesterday you mentioned several times a colonel whose last name you couldn't remember. You thought that perhaps he was called Pavlovic. I would like now to play Exhibit 125, which we saw yesterday. Would you please watch this video excerpt and tell us whether you recognise this Colonel Pavlovic and let's see whether we can identify him closer. This was the excerpt showing the negotiations in Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The officer in question is the one on the left side of the picture in the middle -- on the table, in the middle of the JNA delegation. That's the officer I was referring to. I don't know if he was a Pukovnik or a Potpukovnik. I'm not -- I cannot recall his name precisely, I think it was Pavlovic, but that's the officer I was referring to. This one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the officer. Let us identify him. This is Colonel Pavkovic, Nebojsa Pavkovic. So you were close.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not bad after 14 years, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In this same excerpt that we can see now, are we now seeing the three Croatian representatives who came to negotiate?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you just a bit ago, and then you said you didn't remember on the 20th of November who gave the statement, who was the first to give a statement, after an argument broke out between Sljivancanin and the ICRC representative. You said that you didn't remember who was the first one to do that. Let me give you the position of my client. You confirmed that Mr. Bell was there. My client claims that after Mr. Bell heard what Mr. Borsinger stated, he asked from Mr. Sljivancanin to respond to Mr. Borsinger's allegations, and that his statement, that is to say the statement of my client, was a reaction to the statement given by the ICRC representative. Do you think this is possible?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it's also possible the other way around. I don't have a precise recollection, but it is certainly a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that on the 19th, 20th, 18th there were numerous representatives of various media, electronic media, press, and so on, and that there was an ITN representative there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were not -- I would not call it numerous, no. Most of the journalists were stuck in Belgrade. That was one of the things I noticed about those days, that there were relatively few journalists there, but those that I am aware that were there was a team from the BBC with Martin Bell as the correspondent, a team from ITN with Michael Nicholson as the correspondent and then, as I recall, a number of Serb journalists. But not a large number. It was not numerous, it was a relatively small group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us what is ITN? What kind of an outlet is it?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: ITN is -- stands for Independent Television News. It was part of the first commercial television launched in Britain in the 1950s. I -- they were -- they are terrestrial, not satellite, and they are the competition in Britain for the BBC, which is the state broadcaster.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Alex Thompson mean anything to you in terms of him being an ITN reporter?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. He was at the time working for channel 4 news rather than for the main ITN bulletin which went out on the ITV channel. Channel 4 is a separate channel with a -- rather long on news that goes out once a day, I believe it's 7.00. I'm aware that Mr. Thompson -- and I think I actually mentioned him in my testimony to the Court yesterday, had been in Vukovar prior to our visit there on the 12th of November and that Mr. Sljivancanin actually mentioned having been with Mr. Thompson before that date and that Mr. Thompson had been in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've concluded my cross-examination. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just a few questions and then one clarification from the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I will start on the 19th. What route did you take leaving Vukovar going to Belgrade on the 19th November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, the same route as we took when entering Vukovar on the 19th of November; that would have been through Negoslavci, Oriolik, Tovarnik, Sid, and then the highway to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And when you arrived to Belgrade, can you remember if it was daylight, dusk, or dark at the time?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You think that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Could it --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was almost certainly dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Why do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly because it was November and we would have arrived there at around 6.00 or possibly a little later, but around that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. On the 20th, when you returned -- when you entered Vukovar, did you then -- were you then stopped by any APC on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: On the bridge in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember being on a bridge in Vukovar at all on the 20th. We would have -- we would have entered, again driving Tovarnik, Oriolik, Negoslavci, and into Vukovar, and I don't remember crossing a bridge. The only bridge I ever crossed to get to was the bridge at Erdut to cross the Danube, but we didn't have to do that if you came on the southern route. And as far as being stopped at Erdut on the bridge there was definitely a check-point. Yes, we would have had to go through check-points again on the 20th to reach Vukovar and show that we had permission to enter the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And I would like to have a clarification from the Defence for Mr. Sljivancanin. Can we take it that the Defence of Mr. Sljivancanin accept that Mr. Sljivancanin met the ICRC delegate for -- on the 18th November 1991, following the negotiation on that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can cannot accept what was just proposed by my learned friend because Mr. van Lynden described the contact between my client and the ICRC representative in quite a different light than what is now being proposed by the OTP. Therefore, we cannot accept this as an undisputed fact. Mr. van Lynden is still here; we can ask him to give further explanations as to how he saw Mr. Sljivancanin. And based on what he said, I took it that he knew absolutely nothing about the contact between Mr. Sljivancanin and the ICRC representative.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I would like to ask a few questions to the witness on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: On the 9 -- on the 18th November, can you once again describe what you were encountering that day in terms of this specific topic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I recall meeting Mr. Sljivancanin and ICRC representative in Negoslavci before the negotiations took part, and in fact being told by Mr. Sljivancanin, who we had met earlier, that those negotiations were to take place not in Negoslavci but elsewhere and then being told to follow in a convoy with JNA vehicles and the ICRC delegate to the white farm-house that we've also discussed during the past two days. I am not certain whether Mr. Sljivancanin was at the negotiations themselves, and I cannot say with certainty whether I saw Mr. Sljivancanin talking to the ICRC delegate after the negotiations, but I certainly saw the two of them talking before the negotiations on the 18th of November in the village of Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you're saying "before," how -- how -- how -- can you say -- before, how close to the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I mean, this was just before the convoy drove away to the farm-house where the negotiations took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. And did you take any video of that? Did you film anything of that incident or that event?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I don't recall using it. I think the only video that we used that day of the negotiations was of the pictures the cameraman took inside the farm-house. But it is quite possible that the cameraman also filmed those talks on the road at Negoslavci. I'm not sure whether that was the case or not, but I am absolutely positive that I did meet Mr. Sljivancanin that day and he was talking to the ICRC delegate. But as I say, where I am certain is that it happened in Negoslavci before the negotiations. I'm not sure whether it happened during or after the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I would like to show a video, please, and that is with an ERN number for the video 00000686 and the 65 ter number is 311. And this is an extract of a longer, larger piece. And I want the witness to have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can immediately describe this. Mr. Sljivancanin is standing there. The ICRC representative is standing there. And the man in the back with the glasses is my producer, the field producer, Zoran Kusovac. I imagine these were not pictures taken by my cameraman but by another cameraman who was there. But these were the pictures that -- this is the event I was referring to, the talks in Negoslavci, the meeting in Negoslavci, prior to the beginning of the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I would like to tender --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Just a minute, please, Ms. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. I'll hear Mr. Lukic. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that my colleague has led this witness's evidence, but I would like to clarify something. This is why I took the floor. We have no objections to have this video excerpt exhibited. We also have no problems in putting forward anything about the contacts between Mr. Sljivancanin and the other person on the 18th. However, this is something, this exhibit is something that the OTP had during the examination-in-chief and they did not opt to use this. In examination-in-chief, Mr. van Lynden did not mention anything about the location of the contacts with my client; it was down now by Ms. Tuma. We have not had a chance to cross-examine on this issue. This is why we would like to be allowed to put a question to the issue in order to clarify this additional issue raised by the Prosecution now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, my recollection is always subject to correction, but it is my recollection that the meeting at Negoslavci was specifically mentioned in the course of the evidence in chief of the witness on the 18th, and it was the lack of cross-examination, particularly by your Defence team, in respect of the evidence about that which has led Mrs. Tuma to seek to have clarified whether you were accepting, unquestionably, the evidence. And it's because the answer is given: No, you were not, that she is now proceeding to tender this piece of video.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully understand Mrs. Tuma's approach, but I think that the misunderstanding stems from one fact, and nobody asked the witness about this, namely, were negotiations held in Negoslavci. Based on the examination-in-chief and based on the answers obtained during the cross-examination, it is indisputable that Mr. Sljivancanin met with Mr. Borsinger on the 18th before Negoslavci; however, the negotiations were not held in Negoslavci. This is something that we wanted to clarify, and the witness clearly stated that they went from that location to negotiations. That's all I wanted to clarify, otherwise everything else is indisputable. This is something that the Prosecutor can clarify with the witness now, and there will be no further problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There should be no difficulty. I think the evidence in chief yesterday was clear. I remember picturing the drive in vehicles to a white farm-house from Negoslavci. That, at least, is my recollection, faulty as it often is. Mrs. Tuma, you seek to tender the video extract?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will be Exhibit Number 140.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Finally a question to Witness van Lynden to clarify so there's no misunderstanding on this issue.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We arrived in Negoslavci. There we met Mr. Sljivancanin. There we also met the ICRC delegate; they met each other and spoke to each other. We were told that negotiations would take place elsewhere, and we were told to take -- become part of a convoy that went to these negotiations. The drive, which I have been asked about today, took around 10 or 15 minutes. It was to a white farm-house. That's where the negotiations took place. The only thing I can say absolutely is that I remember absolutely and that the pictures bear out is that we saw and met Mr. Sljivancanin in Negoslavci, that we met the ICRC delegate, and that the two gentlemen met each other in Negoslavci. I cannot, with precision, recall whether Mr. Sljivancanin was later present at the negotiations or after the negotiations and whether he spoke to the ICRC delegate then.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I'm done, so thank you so much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Tuma. You'll be pleased to know, sir, that that brings us to the end of your evidence. The Chamber would express its gratitude for your attendance and for the assistance that you've been able to give us. You may of course now go and do what you will.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Back to work is what it's called, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While you're changing batons there, could I mention that in the course of yesterday Defence counsel, I think it was Mr. Vasic, particularly mentioned a matter that had been hanging over from last year, that is a document that was offered as an exhibit but was marked for identification pending examination of the authenticity. He indicated yesterday for the Defence, as I understand it, that there was no question now of the authenticity and that the document might be received as an exhibit. Can that be attended to at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'm very grateful. It's General Raseta's signature was the signature that was in question. It was marked for identification, I presume there was no dispute, and now it would become an exhibit. I'm afraid I can't remember which exhibit it was; I'm sure Mr. Vasic will know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm looking to the backs of the heads of the court officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's precisely why I got up to my feet. This was document MFI40. This is precisely the document with the disputed signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. The document MFI40 will become Exhibit 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. The next witness is a protected witness and is available and is in a room to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The technical people tell us that it will take at least ten minutes to prepare the sound distortion system for the witness. So we will need now to adjourn to enable that to be done before we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. --- Break taken at 6.24 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good evening, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is offered to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As Your Honour is aware, this a protected witness, also with voice and visual distortion. May I initially, please, tender the -- what I will call a confidential document to this witness to confirm the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I make an application, please, for that document to become an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be an exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be exhibit hundred -- number 141 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The pseudonym here is P-031.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness 31, might I just deal with a number of statements that you made about the incidents at Vukovar. Now, I think it's right that you have with you in a small plastic package a number of statements. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And just for completeness sake and understanding, this is a package of statements which the Defence have had disclosed and I want to deal with them by way of sequence in very shortened form to explain how they were compiled. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness statement, the page number is 00085845 for the court record, and the witness and I call it "statement 1." That was a statement I think that was compiled on the 27th of July, 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is a short statement, one page and about a third. And I think it was released in Zagreb. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have had an opportunity of reading that statement. It is a short statement. In general terms, does it outline the detail of the allegations or the evidence that you will subsequently give?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: Yes, it does, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you can answer questions from the Defence and indeed the Court about that statement. Let us move on to the next document which, for the court record, is 00320131. It is a document of the -- of this Tribunal. It is in typed form, but it is not signed by you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that statement is dated the 21st of June, 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, with regard to that statement, there was an interviewer or an investigator called Dzuro. Do you remember that, that particular investigator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The statement is nine pages long. Now, why did you not sign it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: I did not sign it because at the time I did not agree to appear here at the Tribunal and testify. I had an agreement with Mr. Dzuro, because that's what he had asked for, to give him an account of what had occurred in Vukovar. This was a statement which did not have the nature of an official document, and that was the reason I did not sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's equally correct to say, however, that there was attached to that document what I will call annex A and annex B. They are two drawings. Annex A is at page 00320191, and annex B on 00320193. Is that right that the document has attached to it drawings which were completed by yourself and Mr. Dzuro?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, may I move then to the document that you did sign. I call it "statement 3." That is on the following page number; it is 00400275. And the statement is dated the 25th and 26th of April, 1996. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that is a document that was signed by you as being an accurate record of what had happened to you in what I will call the Vukovar incident. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then finally, I think it's right to say that you had been asked to give evidence in the case of Mr. Dokmanovic, and that you refused to give evidence in that trial. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you, in shortened form, please tell us why it was you did not want to give evidence in the trial of Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: In the Dokmanovic trial, I believed there was not a sufficient number of other statements. I did not see this gentleman and I was not able to identify this gentleman; however, other people told me that he had been present at Ovcara. It was at the insistence of Mr. Dzuro, who was in charge of the investigation, that I agreed to state everything that I experienced and suffered as well as saw and heard at the time. I believed, just by virtue of being heard some stories from others, I was not at the time sufficiently qualified to give evidence before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And perhaps to assist all parties, again you can be asked questions on it. The conversation statement with Mr. Dzuro did implicate Mr. Dokmanovic, but in your statement which was subsequently compiled by you, you indicated that you could not give direct evidence against Mr. Dokmanovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I then -- now I move off from these statements and deal with one or two matters in the remaining time. I'd like to deal, please, in general terms -- I think it's right to say that in November 1991 you were in Vukovar, a resident in Vukovar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you at any time go to the hospital in Vukovar in the middle of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Prior to going to the hospital - and I do not wish to know your address - where had you been located or living?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: In Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And prior to moving to the Vukovar hospital, what were the conditions like that you were living in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: Well, we had been living under very difficult conditions. The war had already begun. There had already been a lot of firing. It was risky to go out and to move around, go just about anywhere you would have needed to go under normal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why did you go to the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: I went to the Vukovar Hospital because my work dictated so. I had a work assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: After the -- the fall of Vukovar, where were you then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: After the fall of Vukovar, I was inside the shelter in my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you leave that shelter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: Yes. I left the shelter on the 19th of November, 1991. I went to the hospital, to the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why did you go to the Vukovar Hospital on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: I went to the Vukovar Hospital because we had been told once we had left the shelter that those who wished to leave for Serbia should go to the parking lot near the Vukovar market, and those who wished to go to Croatia should go to the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you went to the Vukovar Hospital, where did you believe that you were going to be evacuated to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: I believed - and this was the gist of what we had been told - that we would be evacuated to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate how many people had gone to the Vukovar Hospital by the 19th with the belief that they were going to be evacuated to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: On the 19th of November, 1991, when I reached the hospital, there were very many civilians there, residents of the town of Vukovar. As for an estimate, I think I'd be hard-put to be very specific about this. All I know is that those people who were at the hospital, who happened to be at the hospital on that day, throughout that afternoon and until late at night, these people were being taken away in lorries to a collection place called Velepromet Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you went to the Vukovar Hospital, did you go alone or with anyone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: I went with my wife, but there were other people who came with us, those who had been in the shelter with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: I stayed in the Vukovar Hospital that entire day and the entire night, until the morning of the 20th. It was about 7.30 or 8.00 the next morning that we were requested to leave the hospital building and assemble outside in the hospital yard. It was from there that we were loaded on to buses that had already been waiting for us in Gunduliceva Street. They took us from there to the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would just like to slow the pace down a little. Can we deal, please, with the conditions in the hospital on the evening of the 19th and the morning of the 20th. Can you, in general terms, describe to the Court what the situation was like in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: The situation in the hospital was difficult on the 19th, and later on when many of the people there had already left for Velepromet, there was still many wounded and sick in the hospital as well as some of the staff who were not medical staff, but rather just help workers, employees of the hospital. There is also the fact that in addition to the employees, the medical and non-medical staff, some of their family members were allowed to stay in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to recollect where it was you stayed in the hospital on the evening of the 19th and the early morning and morning of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: On the 19th when I reached the hospital, I was put in the x-ray room. This is on the ground floor -- or rather, in the cellar of the hospital building. I spent the night there, and next morning between 7.30 and 8.00 I went outside together with everyone else at the -- taking the back exit of the hospital building. There were JNA soldiers waiting for us there, and they started separating the men from the women and children. The men went to the left and the rest went to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just deal with the x-ray dark-room which you have mentioned. Can you remember the names of any people who were in that same room with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: I can. Throughout that night with me and my wife in that room Dr. Aleksandra Kajba, Dr. Ana Matos, Dr. Vera Kutuzovic-Martic. An x-ray engineer called Adam Ivankovac and his wife Viktoria. Mr. Emil Cakalic and his wife. There was an elderly married couple there who were the parents of Dr. Bosanac's husband. The man's name was Dragutin and I'm not sure about the lady. They were an elderly married couple. There was another x-ray engineer there called Milicko Vukovic. There was a photographer there called Tomislav Mihovic. There were two ladies there, Marija Rehak and Zdenka Zulj, as well as another man who had worked as an electrician for the hospital. His name was Goran Vidos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just ask this one question and then I will stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know if the people you have mentioned here, in this room, whether they -- any of those people travelled with you to the JNA barracks or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And just for completeness, who are the ones that you recollect went to the JNA barracks, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031
utterances.text: Among the persons I have just mentioned as being with me in the x-ray rooms, in the dark-rooms, Mihovic Tomislav and Goran Vidos were later taken with me, first to the barracks and then eventually to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Perhaps that -- perhaps that's an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We have reached 7.00, which is the time we must finish for the day. We will continue the evidence tomorrow at 2.15. We'd be grateful if you would return then. Thank you. We will now adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of January, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
